To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the administration of donor blood before transplantation induces a long-lasting state of immunological unresponsiveness to the donor kidney, despite a rapid and substantial leukocytic infiltrate and a large increase in both class I and II MHC antigene expression within the graft.

pretransplant blood transfusions prolong allograft survival despite an accelerated and increased cellular infiltrate into the graft and an accelerated induction of both class II and class I MHC antigens.
preoperative transfusion produces long-term allograft survival despite a rapid and extensive induction of donor class I and II MHC antigen and an accelerated cellular infiltrate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the immunologic basis of blood transfusion-induced graft survival.
the immunologic mechanisms of enhanced allograft survival in the rat.

the mechanisms of prolonged survival induced by preoperative blood transfusions and the immunologic basis for the paradoxical finding of enhanced grafts showing a more rapid and extensive leukocyte infiltrate and induction of both donor MHC class I and class I MHC antigens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
blood transfusions do not prevent rejection but rather suppress it.
the mechanism of prolonged survival is not due to a failure of the immune system to mount an effective rejection response.

the enhanced state of the allograft, in this model, is characterized by an accelerated and extensive cellular infiltration of both donor and host origin, and a more rapid induction and expression of both donor class II and class I MHC antigens, which are accompanied by an accelerated disappearance of donor interstitium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the administration of donor blood before transplantation produces a profound and sustained suppression of allograft rejection.
pretransplant blood transfusions produce an enhanced graft survival in the RT1a into RT1c strain combination, and this is due to the induction of a state of specific immunological unresponsiveness.

preoperative transfusion with donor blood induces an accelerated rejection process, which is associated with a more rapid infiltration of the graft by donor-reactive cells, an accelerated induction of both donor MHC class I and class I antigens, and the rapid elimination of donor interstitial elements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of donor blood in the recipient before transplant can have a profound effect on the immune system.
pretransplant blood transfusion can induce a state of immunologic tolerance in the recipient to the donor organ.
preoperative blood transfusions are not only effective in preventing acute rejection but also have a profound effect on the immune response in a number of ways.
